newsitem.title: USA: SOYBEANS--Tracking soybeans in food a tough job.
newsitem.headline: SOYBEANS--Tracking soybeans in food a tough job.

text.p: Tracking a soybean's path from the field through the processing plant and into hundreds of processed foods is virtually impossible, industry experts say.
But that is what some consumer groups are asking in order to ensure that food products made from new genetically altered soybeans can be identified and carry consumer-advice labels.
"It's not like a carrot," said Karen Marshall, a spokeswoman for Monsanto Co. "They (soybean products) are in candy bars, cookies, crackers. It's virtually everywhere."

A coalition of U.S. consumer and environmental groups announced on Monday a global boycott of genetically altered corn and soybeans and targeted 10 foods from Coca-Cola Co to McDonald's Corp French fries.

The European Union has approved sale of the gene-altered soybeans and has yet to decide on the corn. The technology for the weedkiller-resistant soybean was developed by Monsanto. The corn produces a naturally occuring pesticide to repel the damaging corn borer.
Both crops have U.S. approval for marketing, and industry groups defend them as scientifically safe and no different in substance from conventional ones.
"I think it will be very difficult for the market to find a way to sort GMO's (genetically modified organisms)," said a soybean merchandiser who declined to be named.

"The calls for labeling are begging the question because that presumes there is some difference...and that just isn't true," said Sheldon Hauch, president of the National Oilseed Processors Association.

Some grain merchandisers contacted by Reuters said they are discussing a plan to offer supplies of non-genetically altered soybeans. But the plan may rely largely on a farmer's word whether the soybeans are from conventional seed.
Soybeans from different fields are frequently mixed by farmers and are mixed again at grain elevators and again at points throughout the marketing chain.
A 60-lb bushel of soybeans, when processed or "crushed," typically yields about 48 lbs of meal and 11 lbs of soybean oil.

The first is widely used as a protein supplement for livestock. The second is used for for human consumption in cooking oil, margarine, mayonnaise, salad oils, and processed foods and as an industrial component of hundreds of products ranging from newpaper ink and plastics to adhesives.
